subsection: 3. How the EU influences the Irish economy

notes.h: Ireland's net position in the EU budget
points: Ireland was a net recipient of EU budget money from joining on 1 January 1973 until about 2014, receiving over €40 billion more than it paid in, mostly through the CAP.
Ireland became a net contributor in 2014, the first time since joining, because of its economic growth.
Advantages: access to the single market, foreign direct investment, CAP payments, structural funds for infrastructure, social and equality laws, and free movement to work and study.
Costs: loss of control over some policies, such as fishing and farm prices; net contributions to the EU budget since 2014; and competition from lower-cost members.
Enlargement's effects on Ireland are covered in The complexity of regions (ii).

notes.h: Origins and aims of the CAP
notes.b: The Common Agricultural Policy was launched in 1962.
points: Its aims, set out in the Treaty of Rome, were to raise farm productivity, give farmers a fair standard of living, stabilise markets, secure food supplies and provide reasonable prices for consumers.
The CAP was once the largest part of the EU budget. It still takes about a third of the budget (2021-27).
Guaranteed (intervention) prices were set above world levels, and intervention buying took up surpluses.
Export subsidies and import levies supported the system.
Results: overproduction, shown by the butter mountains and wine lakes of the 1970s and 1980s, high cost, and dumping of surpluses on world markets.

notes.h: Effects of the CAP on Ireland after 1973
points: Farm prices and incomes rose sharply.
A guaranteed market opened for beef and dairy.
Farms modernised with machinery, fertiliser, silage, land drainage and farm buildings, in what is remembered as the golden age of the 1970s.
Milk quotas, introduced in 1984, capped each farm's milk output to cut surpluses. They held back Irish dairying for 30 years.
The quotas were abolished on 1 April 2015; the last quota year ended on 31 March 2015.
Irish milk output rose from about 5.5 billion litres in 2014 to about 8.3 billion litres in 2020.
From 2013 to 2023 dairy cow numbers rose about 41% and milk output about 56% (EPA, from CSO data).
Expansion was strongest in the south, especially Munster.
The MacSharry reform of 1992, led by Ray MacSharry, EU Agriculture Commissioner from Sligo, replaced price cuts with direct payments and introduced set-aside.
Agenda 2000 made rural development the second pillar of the CAP.
The Fischler reform, agreed in 2003, decoupled payments from production.
The Single Farm Payment began in 2005 and was replaced by the Basic Payment Scheme from 2015.
Cross-compliance links payments to environmental and animal-welfare rules.
Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan is worth about €9.8 billion from EU and national funds, with about 45% for environmental and climate measures.
Basic Income Support for Sustainability (BISS) is worth about €3.6 billion. The eco-scheme is worth about €1.5 billion, 25% of direct payments.
Convergence raises every payment entitlement to at least 85% of the national average.
Payments for young farmers and the ACRES agri-environment scheme are included in the plan.
Areas of Natural Constraint (ANC) payments support farms on disadvantaged land.
REPS, the Rural Environment Protection Scheme, ran from 1994 to 2009 as an agri-environment scheme.
LEADER, from 1991, funds local rural enterprise such as farm diversification, rural tourism and crafts.
Grants support forestry and young farmers.
The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted 135,037 farms, down about 3% on 2010, with an average size of about 33 hectares.
On a third (33%) of farms the holder was aged 65 or over; only 7% of holders were under 35.
The main farm types are dairy, cattle (beef) rearing, sheep, tillage and mixed. Specialist beef is the most common type.
Stable farm incomes and a guaranteed market.
Modernisation of farms and food quality standards.
Environmental schemes and support for rural communities.
Dependence on direct payments is high for many beef and sheep farms, which is a limit as well as a support.
Payments have historically favoured bigger farmers, so most of the money went to a minority.
Dependence on subsidies and heavy bureaucracy and inspections.
Intensification has damaged water quality through nitrates and raised greenhouse gas emissions as the dairy herd grew.
The number of farms has fallen and farmers are ageing; small western farms remain uneconomic.
Trade deals such as EU-Mercosur, which concluded in December 2024 and was opposed by Irish farm organisations, are feared to undercut Irish beef.
The Nitrates Directive of 1991 limits the organic nitrogen that can be spread per hectare.
Ireland has a derogation that allows higher stocking on intensive farms, conditional on water quality. EU environmental rules therefore shape farming directly.

notes.h: Aims and principles of the CFP
points: The Common Fisheries Policy was agreed in full in 1983. It creates a common pond of EU waters, giving all members' fleets equal access beyond coastal limits.
Its aim is to conserve fish stocks for the long term.
Ireland had to share its rich waters with much larger fleets, notably those of Spain, France and the Netherlands. Spain and Portugal joined in 1986.
Total Allowable Catches (TACs) are set each December by EU fisheries ministers and divided into national quotas using fixed shares.
A coastal band of 12 nautical miles is reserved mainly for local boats.
Days-at-sea limits, mesh sizes, closed areas and closed seasons control fishing effort.
The Hague Preferences, agreed in 1976, give Ireland a smaller cut when TACs fall, in recognition of its coastal communities' dependence on fishing.
Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is Ireland's largest fishing port by volume and value, specialising in pelagic fish: mackerel, herring and blue whiting.
The other Fishery Harbour Centres are Castletownbere (Co. Cork), Ros an Mhíl (Rossaveel, Co. Galway), Dingle (Co. Kerry), Howth (Co. Dublin) and Dunmore East (Co. Waterford).
Bord Iascaigh Mhara (BIM) is the state seafood development agency.
Processing and fishing jobs sustain peripheral coastal areas.
EU funding for boats, harbours and processing plants, now through the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund.
Conservation aims protect stocks over the long term.
Access to EU seafood markets.
The Hague Preferences protect Ireland's share when quotas are cut.
Ireland's quota share is small relative to the size and richness of its waters.
Overfishing and stock collapses have occurred despite the CFP.
Discards, the throwing back of dead fish, were common until the landing obligation.
Decommissioning of boats and job losses in coastal communities.
Quota cuts under Brexit.
The reform was agreed in 2013. It introduced a landing obligation, which bans discarding, phased in between 2015 and 2019.
It aims to fish at maximum sustainable yield.
Depletion of fish stocks as an economic and environmental conflict is covered in Conflicts between economic interests and environmental interests.
The EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement from 1 January 2021 transferred EU quota to the UK.
Ireland lost about 26% of its mackerel quota. The government's Seafood Task Force valued the annual quota loss at about €43 million by 2026.
Irish ministers said Ireland's losses were about double those of other EU fleets in proportion.
The Brexit Adjustment Reserve gave Ireland about €1 billion, the largest share of the EU-wide reserve.
A €25.6 million pelagic support scheme was funded from the reserve, and a voluntary permanent cessation (decommissioning) scheme ran in 2022-23.

notes.h: Origins of the regional development funds
points: The EU has regional inequality, and Ireland was a poor, peripheral member in 1973.
The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) was set up in 1975 to fund infrastructure, enterprise, research and innovation in poorer regions.
The Structural Funds (ERDF, the European Social Fund and the farm guidance fund) doubled after the 1988-89 reform, to prepare poorer regions for the single market.
Ireland was a single Objective 1 region from 1989 to 1999, because its income per head was below 75% of the EU average. National Development Plans were co-financed by the EU.

The Cohesion Fund began in 1993-94 under the Maastricht Treaty. It serves states with income below 90% of the EU average, namely Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Greece, and funds transport and environmental projects.
Ireland stopped qualifying for the Cohesion Fund as its income rose in the 2000s.
Ireland was split into two regions. The Border, Midland and Western (BMW) region kept Objective 1 status.
The Southern and Eastern region was in transition, not Objective 1.
Roads, including inter-urban motorways and bypasses, and public transport.
Water and wastewater treatment, ports, airports and broadband.
Research centres and enterprise support.
Better access for peripheral regions, attraction of foreign direct investment, and a contribution to the Celtic Tiger.
ERDF regional programmes are run by the regional assemblies. Two regional programmes are worth about €853 million in total, of which about €396 million comes from the EU.
The Northern and Western Region was reclassified from a more developed to a transition region, because its income relative to the EU average fell.
The Southern and Eastern and Midland regions remain more developed regions.
Three regional assemblies have operated since 2015.
PEACE PLUS (2021-27) and INTERREG support the border region. Their facts are in The complexity of regions (i).
The Just Transition Fund (2021-27) targets the Midlands peat region after Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting for electricity.
The funds helped Ireland converge with EU incomes and modernised its infrastructure.
The gap between the Dublin-centred east and the Northern and Western region has persisted.
As a wealthy member, Ireland now receives far less, and EU regional funds go mainly to eastern Europe, an effect of enlargement.
The ESF was set up by the Treaty of Rome in 1957 and is the oldest structural fund.
It improves employment, skills and social inclusion.
The ESF co-financed training through FÁS (1988-2013), replaced in 2013 by SOLAS and 16 Education and Training Boards.
Youthreach, begun in 1989, helps early school-leavers. Post-Leaving Cert courses, apprenticeships and back-to-education schemes are also co-financed.
Programmes target the long-term unemployed, people with disabilities, Travellers and women returning to work.
The skilled workforce created this way helped attract foreign direct investment.
The Employment, Inclusion, Skills and Training (EIST) programme for 2021-2027 is worth about €1.08 billion: about €508 million from the EU and about €573 million national.
It was launched in March 2023.

Priorities: about €500 million for social inclusion, about €280 million for upskilling and lifelong learning, and over €180 million for employment, mainly of young people and the long-term unemployed.
The EGF was set up in 2007 to retrain workers made redundant by shifts in global trade.

In 2009 the EU approved about €14.8 million to help about 2,400 former Dell and supplier workers in the Limerick area. Dell had announced in January 2009 that it was moving manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź in Poland.
Waterford Crystal workers also received EGF support.
The civil service marriage bar ended in 1973. Irish equality laws followed EEC directives: the Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and the Employment Equality Act 1977.
The Organisation of Working Time Act 1997, which applied the EU Working Time Directive, set an average maximum working week of 48 hours.
EU directives also set rules on health and safety, maternity and parental leave, and the rights of part-time workers.
Irish people can live and work anywhere in the EU.
The Erasmus student exchange programme, from 1987, lets students study abroad.
EU workers came to Ireland after 2004; their effects are covered in The complexity of regions (ii).
The ESF raised skills and employment, especially in the 1990s.
Some training schemes were criticised as poorly targeted.
Social funding is now much smaller relative to the size of the Irish economy.

keyTerms.definition: The EU policy, launched in 1962, that supports farm incomes, markets and food supply through payments and rural development.
A guaranteed minimum price for farm produce, set above world levels, at which the EU bought surpluses.
A limit on the milk each farm could produce, used from 1984 to 2015 to cut surpluses.
Separating farm payments from the amount a farmer produces, as introduced by the 2003 Fischler reform.
The EU policy that manages fishing in EU waters through shared access, catch limits and conservation rules.
The maximum tonnage of a fish stock that may be caught in a year, divided into national quotas.
The rule, phased in from 2015 to 2019, that requires all catches to be landed rather than discarded.
The EU funds, including the ERDF and ESF, that reduce differences between regions and social groups.
A region whose income per head is below 75% of the EU average, and so qualifies for the largest EU structural funding.
An EU fund from 1993-94 for states with income below 90% of the EU average, financing transport and environmental projects.
The oldest EU structural fund, set up in 1957 to improve employment, skills and social inclusion.
An EU fund, set up in 2007, that retrains workers made redundant by shifts in global trade.

factCards.term: EU membership for Ireland: advantages, costs and budget position
factCards.definition: Advantages: single market access, FDI, CAP payments, structural funds, equality laws, free movement. Costs: lost control of fishing and farm prices; lower-cost competitors; net contributor since 2014, after over €40 billion net received from 1973.

factCards.term: CAP: launch date, five aims and share of the EU budget
factCards.definition: Launched in 1962. Treaty of Rome aims: raise farm productivity; a fair standard of living for farmers; stable markets; secure food supplies; reasonable prices for consumers. It still takes about a third of the EU budget (2021–27).

factCards.term: The early CAP (1962–1992): how it worked and what went wrong
factCards.definition: Intervention prices above world levels, intervention buying of surpluses, export subsidies and import levies. Results: overproduction (butter mountains and wine lakes in the 1970s and 1980s), high cost, and surpluses dumped on world markets.

factCards.term: CAP: positive effects on Irish farming since 1973
factCards.definition: Prices and incomes rose sharply in the 1970s golden age; a guaranteed market for beef and dairy; modernisation (machinery, fertiliser, silage, drainage, farm buildings); food quality standards; environmental schemes; support for rural communities.

factCards.term: Milk quotas: dates, and what happened after abolition
factCards.definition: In force from 1984 to 1 April 2015, they held back dairying for 30 years. Milk output then rose from about 5.5 billion litres (2014) to about 8.3 billion (2020); over 2013–2023 cows rose about 41% and milk about 56% (EPA), especially in Munster.

factCards.term: CAP reforms in order, from MacSharry to the Basic Payment Scheme
factCards.definition: MacSharry 1992 (Ray MacSharry, from Sligo): direct payments in place of price support, plus set-aside. Agenda 2000: rural development became the second pillar. Fischler 2003: decoupling; Single Farm Payment 2005; Basic Payment Scheme 2015.

factCards.term: Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan 2023–2027: key figures and schemes
factCards.definition: About €9.8 billion (EU and national), about 45% for environment and climate; BISS about €3.6 billion; eco-scheme about €1.5 billion (25% of direct payments); convergence to at least 85% of the national average; ACRES; young farmer and ANC payments.

factCards.term: CAP rural development: two named Irish schemes
factCards.definition: REPS (Rural Environment Protection Scheme), 1994 to 2009, an agri-environment scheme; LEADER, from 1991, funding local rural enterprise such as farm diversification, rural tourism and crafts. Grants also support forestry and young farmers.

factCards.term: Irish farms in the Census of Agriculture 2020
factCards.definition: 135,037 farms, down about 3% on 2010; average size about 33 hectares; on 33% of farms the holder was 65 or over and only 7% were under 35. Farm types: dairy, cattle (beef) rearing, sheep, tillage and mixed; specialist beef is the most common.

factCards.term: CAP: five negative effects on Ireland
factCards.definition: Payments favoured bigger farmers; subsidy dependence, bureaucracy and inspections; intensification harmed water (the 1991 Nitrates Directive caps organic nitrogen per hectare) and raised emissions; fewer, older farmers; Mercosur fears for beef.

factCards.term: CFP: when agreed, its main principle, and why Ireland lost out
factCards.definition: Agreed in full in 1983, it makes EU waters a common pond, open to all fleets beyond coastal limits, and conserves stocks. Ireland had to share its rich waters with larger fleets from Spain, France and the Netherlands; Spain and Portugal joined in 1986.

factCards.term: How the CFP controls fishing: five tools, and the Hague Preferences
factCards.definition: TACs set each December by fisheries ministers, split into national quotas by fixed shares; a 12-nautical-mile band mainly for local boats; days-at-sea limits; mesh sizes; closed areas and seasons. The Hague Preferences (1976) protect Ireland when TACs fall.

factCards.term: Ireland's fishing ports: the largest and the other harbour centres
factCards.definition: Killybegs, Co. Donegal, is the largest by volume and value, landing pelagic mackerel, herring and blue whiting. Other Fishery Harbour Centres: Castletownbere, Ros an Mhíl, Dingle, Howth and Dunmore East. BIM is the state seafood development agency.

factCards.term: CFP: four positive effects on Ireland
factCards.definition: EU funding for boats, harbours and processing plants, now through the European Maritime, Fisheries and Aquaculture Fund; conservation to protect stocks long-term; access to EU seafood markets; the Hague Preferences protect Ireland's share when quotas are cut.

factCards.term: CFP: negative effects on Ireland, and the 2013 reform
factCards.definition: Ireland's quota share is small relative to its rich waters; overfishing and stock collapses; decommissioning and lost coastal jobs; discards, until the 2013 reform's landing obligation (phased in 2015–2019) and maximum sustainable yield goal.

factCards.term: Brexit and Irish fishing: what Ireland lost
factCards.definition: The Trade and Cooperation Agreement (2021) moved quota to the UK: Ireland lost about 26% of its mackerel quota, and the Seafood Task Force valued its annual quota loss at about €43 million by 2026. Irish ministers said Ireland's losses were about double other EU fleets' in proportion.

factCards.term: Brexit Adjustment Reserve: how it helped Irish fishing
factCards.definition: Ireland received about €1 billion, the largest share of the EU-wide reserve. It funded a €25.6 million pelagic support scheme and a voluntary permanent cessation (decommissioning) scheme in 2022–23.

factCards.term: ERDF: when it began, its purposes, and the 1988–89 reform
factCards.definition: Set up in 1975 to cut regional inequality by funding infrastructure, enterprise, research and innovation in poorer regions. The Structural Funds (ERDF, ESF, farm guidance fund) doubled after the 1988–89 reform to prepare poorer regions for the single market.

factCards.term: Objective 1 and the Cohesion Fund: Ireland's qualification
factCards.definition: All of Ireland was one Objective 1 region, 1989–1999 (income below 75% of the EU average). The Cohesion Fund (1993/94, Maastricht) funded transport and environment in Ireland, Spain, Portugal and Greece (below 90%); Ireland stopped qualifying in the 2000s.

factCards.term: Ireland's EU regional status in 2000–2006 and 2021–2027
factCards.definition: 2000–06: the BMW region kept Objective 1 status; Southern and Eastern was in transition. 2021–27: Northern and Western became a transition region as its relative income fell; two ERDF programmes, about €853 million (€396 million EU), run by the assemblies.

factCards.term: What EU regional funds built in Ireland, and their mixed results
factCards.definition: Inter-urban motorways and bypasses, public transport, water treatment, ports, airports, broadband, research centres. They opened up the periphery, drew FDI and fed the Celtic Tiger, but the east–west gap persists and funds now go mainly to eastern Europe.

factCards.term: Three other EU funds for Irish regions
factCards.definition: PEACE PLUS (2021–27) and INTERREG support the border region; the Just Transition Fund (2021–27) targets the Midlands peat region after Bord na Móna ended peat harvesting for electricity.

factCards.term: European Social Fund: origin and what it funded in Ireland
factCards.definition: Set up by the Treaty of Rome (1957), the oldest structural fund. In Ireland it co-financed FÁS training (1988–2013; then SOLAS and 16 Education and Training Boards), Youthreach (from 1989), Post-Leaving Cert courses and apprenticeships.

factCards.term: ESF+ EIST programme 2021–2027: value and priorities
factCards.definition: About €1.08 billion (about €508 million EU, €573 million national), launched March 2023: about €500 million for social inclusion, €280 million for upskilling and lifelong learning, over €180 million for jobs for young and long-term unemployed people.

factCards.term: Globalisation Adjustment Fund: the Dell Limerick example
factCards.definition: Set up in 2007. After Dell announced in January 2009 that it was moving manufacturing from Limerick to Łódź, Poland, the EU approved about €14.8 million in 2009 to retrain about 2,400 Dell and supplier workers. Waterford Crystal workers were also helped.

factCards.term: EU social laws that changed Irish workplaces
factCards.definition: Civil service marriage bar ended 1973; Anti-Discrimination (Pay) Act 1974 and Employment Equality Act 1977 followed EEC directives; Organisation of Working Time Act 1997: average 48-hour maximum week; also maternity leave and part-time workers' rights.

questions.prompt: Examine the impact of the Common Agricultural Policy on Irish agriculture.
questions.model: The CAP was launched in 1962 to raise farm productivity, give farmers a fair standard of living, stabilise markets, secure food supplies and provide reasonable prices. Its early system of intervention prices, intervention buying and export subsidies produced butter mountains and wine lakes, high cost and dumping. After 1973 Irish farm prices and incomes rose sharply, a guaranteed market opened for beef and dairy, and farms modernised with machinery, fertiliser, silage and drainage. Milk quotas from 1984 capped output and held back Irish dairying for 30 years, until they were abolished on 1 April 2015; Irish milk output then rose from about 5.5 billion litres in 2014 to about 8.3 billion litres in 2020, and from 2013 to 2023 dairy cow numbers rose about 41%. The MacSharry reform of 1992 replaced price cuts with direct payments; the Fischler reform of 2003 decoupled payments from production, with the Single Farm Payment from 2005 and the Basic Payment Scheme from 2015. Ireland's CAP Strategic Plan for 2023-2027 is worth about €9.8 billion, with about 45% for environmental and climate measures, BISS about €3.6 billion and the eco-scheme about €1.5 billion. REPS ran from 1994 to 2009 and LEADER from 1991 supports rural enterprise. The Census of Agriculture 2020 counted 135,037 farms, averaging about 33 hectares, with a third of holders aged 65 or over and only 7% under 35. Positive effects are stable incomes, modernisation, food quality and environmental schemes. Negative effects are that payments favoured bigger farmers, that dependence on subsidies and bureaucracy grew, that intensification harmed water quality and raised emissions, that farm numbers fell and farmers aged, and that small western farms remain uneconomic. Trade deals such as EU-Mercosur are feared to undercut Irish beef.

questions.prompt: Discuss the impact of the Common Fisheries Policy on the Irish fishing industry.
questions.model: The CFP was agreed in full in 1983 and creates a common pond of EU waters in which all members' fleets have equal access beyond coastal limits. Total Allowable Catches are set each December by EU fisheries ministers and divided into national quotas using fixed shares, with a 12-nautical-mile coastal band reserved mainly for local boats. The Hague Preferences of 1976 protect Ireland's share when TACs fall. Killybegs in Co. Donegal is Ireland's largest fishing port, specialising in pelagic fish such as mackerel, herring and blue whiting, and other Fishery Harbour Centres include Castletownbere, Dingle, Howth and Dunmore East. Positive effects include EU funding for boats, harbours and processing plants, conservation of stocks, access to EU seafood markets, and protection of Ireland's share through the Hague Preferences. Negative effects include a small quota share relative to the size of Irish waters, stock collapses despite the CFP, discards of dead fish until the landing obligation, decommissioning of boats and job losses in coastal communities. The 2013 reform introduced the landing obligation, phased in between 2015 and 2019. Brexit has been costly for Irish fishing: the EU-UK Trade and Cooperation Agreement from 2021 transferred quota to the UK, Ireland lost about 26% of its mackerel quota, and the Seafood Task Force valued the annual loss at about €43 million by 2026. Ireland was the largest beneficiary of the Brexit Adjustment Reserve, about €1 billion, which funded a €25.6 million pelagic support scheme and a decommissioning scheme in 2022-23.

questions.prompt: (i) Name two ways the EU has funded regional or social development in Ireland. (ii) Explain the benefits of each.
questions.model: (i) The EU has funded regional development through the European Regional Development Fund and the Cohesion Fund, and social development through the European Social Fund and the European Globalisation Adjustment Fund. (ii) The ERDF and Cohesion Fund: from 1989 to 1999 the whole of Ireland was a single Objective 1 region, because its income per head was below 75% of the EU average. The funds paid for roads, motorways and bypasses, public transport, water and wastewater treatment, ports, airports and broadband, which improved access for peripheral regions and helped attract foreign direct investment. The Border, Midland and Western region kept Objective 1 status from 2000 to 2006, and the Northern and Western Region became a transition region in 2021-2027. The European Social Fund: since 1957 it has improved employment, skills and social inclusion. In Ireland it co-financed FÁS and later SOLAS training, Youthreach, apprenticeships and programmes for the long-term unemployed, and the EIST programme for 2021-2027, worth about €1.08 billion. Its skilled workforce helped attract investment. The EGF gave about €14.8 million in 2009 to about 2,400 former Dell workers in Limerick, helping them retrain.
